topic: E1.1.2 and E1.2.1 Online financial services and transactional data
scenario:
BrightBank plc is a high-street bank with 200 branches. It is planning to close 150 branches over the next three years and migrate all retail banking services — including current accounts, savings, mortgages and insurance — to a new online platform. The bank will retain 50 branches in major cities to serve customers who cannot or will not use digital services. BrightBank will also use the transactional data generated by online banking to offer personalised financial products to customers.

You should consider:
• The implications for BrightBank of operating predominantly online
• The implications for customers of the branch closure and migration to online banking
• The use of transactional data and targeted marketing of financial products
question:
Evaluate the implications for BrightBank plc and its customers of the move to predominantly online financial services and the use of transactional data for targeted marketing.

You should consider:
• The implications for BrightBank of operating predominantly online
• The implications for customers of the branch closure and migration to online banking
• The use of transactional data and targeted marketing of financial products

indicative_content: IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Significant cost savings: closure of 150 branches reduces rent, rates, staffing and maintenance costs
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Online platform enables 24/7 service without proportional increase in staff costs
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Wider data collection on spending patterns enables personalised product offerings
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Increased revenue through data-driven cross-selling (e.g. offering mortgages to renters, investments to savers)
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Investment required in new digital platform development, security and maintenance
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Significant cybersecurity risks: online banking is a prime target for phishing, fraud and data breaches
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Regulatory compliance with FCA and GDPR requirements
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Reputational risk if digital services fail, are hacked or customers are treated unfairly
IMPLICATIONS FOR BRIGHTBANK — Redundancy costs and HR implications from closing 150 branches
IMPLICATIONS FOR CUSTOMERS — Convenience: 24/7 access from any device without visiting a branch
IMPLICATIONS FOR CUSTOMERS — Digital exclusion: elderly, disabled or rurally isolated customers disadvantaged by branch closures
IMPLICATIONS FOR CUSTOMERS — Loss of face-to-face access for complex needs (mortgages, bereavement, financial hardship)
IMPLICATIONS FOR CUSTOMERS — 50 remaining branches provide some safety net but coverage will be insufficient for many
IMPLICATIONS FOR CUSTOMERS — Security risks: phishing, account takeover, online fraud increase in digital-only environment
TRANSACTIONAL DATA — Enables personalised product recommendations based on actual spending patterns
TRANSACTIONAL DATA — Risk of customers feeling surveilled or manipulated by targeted financial product marketing
TRANSACTIONAL DATA — GDPR: consent required; customers must be able to opt out of marketing
TRANSACTIONAL DATA — Data breach of financial transaction records has severe consequences for customers

CONCLUSION — The move to predominantly online banking offers BrightBank substantial financial and operational benefits; however, the implications for digitally excluded customers are significant and the ethical use of transactional data requires transparent, consent-based practices. A phased approach retaining 50 branches partially addresses inclusion concerns but may not be sufficient. Overall, the strategy is commercially justified but carries significant risks if implementation is poor.

topic: E2.3.2 Questionnaire — advantages and design
scenario: Hilltop Adventure Park is a family attraction with outdoor activities including zip-wires and climbing walls. The management team wants to measure visitor satisfaction and has decided to use a paper questionnaire distributed at the exit gate.
question: Explain two advantages of using a questionnaire to collect visitor satisfaction data at Hilltop Adventure Park.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for each advantage identified and one mark for a linked expansion, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: Questionnaires can be distributed to a large number of visitors quickly and cost-effectively (1) providing a larger, more representative sample of opinions than methods such as interviews (1)
Responses can be collected anonymously (1) which may encourage visitors to give more honest feedback about any negative aspects of their experience (1)
Closed questions with rating scales can be quickly tallied and analysed numerically (1) making it straightforward to identify overall satisfaction scores and trends over time (1)
Questionnaires are completed by visitors at their own pace without requiring staff time for each respondent (1) reducing the labour cost of data collection compared with conducting interviews (1)

topic: E2.6.3 and E2.6.4 Error reduction and functionality
scenario: PowerGrid Energy is a utility company whose engineers use a mobile app to log meter readings and fault reports when visiting customer premises.
question: Describe four ways the PowerGrid mobile app could be designed to reduce errors and ensure good functionality for engineers in the field.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per correctly described feature, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: Drop-down lists for fault type selection to prevent engineers entering invalid codes (1)
Numeric keypad automatically presented when entering meter readings (1)
Range validation check to flag meter readings significantly outside expected bounds for review (1)
GPS auto-populate of location data to reduce manual address entry errors (1)
Offline mode so the app functions when there is no mobile signal, syncing data when connectivity returns (1)
Photo capture integrated with the report form so visual evidence is automatically linked to the correct job record (1)
Mandatory fields that cannot be bypassed to ensure all required data is captured before submission (1)

topic: E1.1.5 Online entertainment — features
scenario: GameVault is an online gaming subscription service that provides access to a library of over 300 games. Players can save progress, connect with friends and earn achievements.
question: Explain two features of GameVault's online entertainment service that encourage customers to maintain their subscription.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award marks for two features with at least one expanded, up to three marks total.
points: Progress saving across devices means players can continue games from where they left off (1) creating a sense of investment that makes cancelling the subscription feel like a loss (1)
Social features such as friend lists and multiplayer modes (1) build a community that adds ongoing value beyond the game library itself (1)
Regular addition of new games to the library (1) gives subscribers a continuing reason to stay as there is always fresh content to discover (1)
Achievement and reward systems (1) provide ongoing goals that keep players engaged and returning to the platform (1)

topic: E2.2 and E2.1.2 Secondary data reliability
scenario: Oakfield Construction is planning to build a new retail development. Before submission of a planning application, the company needs evidence about local population and retail demand.
question: Explain why Oakfield Construction should use more than one secondary data source when gathering evidence for its planning application.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per developed point, up to a maximum of three marks.
points: No single secondary source may have all the data required for a planning application (1)
Using multiple sources allows the findings to be cross-referenced and verified (1) increasing confidence that the data is accurate and not an anomaly from one source (1)
Different sources may provide complementary data (e.g. ONS population statistics alongside local council retail studies) (1) giving a more complete picture of local demand (1)
Individual sources may have limitations, such as outdated figures or a narrow focus (1) which can be identified and compensated for by comparing with other sources (1)

topic: E1.1.1 Online retail — transactional data
scenario: Stonegate Wines is an online wine retailer. It analyses transactional data from its 50,000 customer accounts to plan its stock purchasing and promotions.
question: Explain how Stonegate Wines could use transactional data to improve its stock purchasing decisions.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per developed point, up to a maximum of three marks.
points: Transactional data shows which wines are sold most frequently (1) allowing the buyer to order larger quantities of popular lines to meet demand and avoid stock-outs (1)
Seasonal purchasing trends visible in the data (e.g. sparkling wine sales rising before Christmas) (1) allow the company to increase stock levels ahead of peak periods (1)
Data on which products customers often buy together (1) can inform bundled purchasing decisions and promotional packs (1)
Slow-moving stock identified from transaction data (1) can be discounted or removed from the catalogue to free up warehouse space and cash (1)

topic: E2.6.2 Accessibility — implications
scenario: Salford City Council is launching an online portal for residents to report missed bin collections and apply for parking permits.
question: Explain why Salford City Council must consider accessibility when designing its new online portal.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per developed point, up to a maximum of three marks.
points: Local councils provide services to the whole community, including residents with visual, hearing, motor or cognitive disabilities (1)
Failure to make the portal accessible could prevent disabled residents from accessing services they are entitled to (1) which could constitute a breach of the Equality Act 2010 (1)
Public sector websites in the UK are legally required to meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards (1) so accessibility is both a moral and a legal obligation for the council (1)
An accessible portal reduces the need for telephone or in-person contact for residents who could self-serve digitally (1) improving efficiency and reducing demand on council staff (1)

topic: E1.2.3 Collaborative working — tools and implications
scenario: Ravenswood Publishing produces academic textbooks and journals. Its editorial teams, authors and designers are spread across the UK and work on book projects together using cloud-based tools.
question: Describe four ways that online collaborative tools benefit Ravenswood Publishing's editorial process.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per correctly described benefit, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: Authors and editors can comment on and annotate shared manuscript documents simultaneously without emailing multiple versions (1)
Version history tracking ensures the editorial team can revert to an earlier draft if needed (1)
Project management tools allow progress on each title to be tracked against deadlines by all team members (1)
Video conferencing enables editorial meetings between geographically dispersed authors and editors without travel (1)
Design files shared via cloud storage allow designers to receive immediate feedback from editors on layouts (1)
Instant messaging reduces delays in resolving minor queries between authors and copyeditors (1)

topic: E2.5.2 Validation — comprehensive application
scenario: VitaPlus Pharmacy has launched an online prescription request system. Patients enter their NHS number, name, date of birth, the medication name and quantity required.
question: Explain two validation methods that VitaPlus Pharmacy could apply to its online prescription request form to ensure the data entered by patients is accurate.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for each validation method identified and one mark for a linked explanation of its application, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: A format check on the NHS number field (1) to ensure it is entered as a ten-digit number in the correct pattern (e.g. three digits, space, three digits, space, four digits) (1)
A presence check on all required fields (1) to prevent the patient submitting the request with any mandatory information missing (1)
A range check on the quantity field (1) to ensure the requested quantity is within acceptable limits for a standard prescription (1)
A type check on the NHS number and date of birth fields (1) to ensure only numeric characters are entered rather than letters (1)

topic: E1.1.6 Online booking systems — impact on customer experience
scenario: Amber Veterinary Practice currently takes all appointments by telephone during opening hours. The practice manager is evaluating whether to introduce an online booking system.
question: Explain two ways that introducing an online booking system would improve the experience of clients at Amber Veterinary Practice.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for each benefit identified and one mark for a linked expansion, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: Clients can book appointments at any time of day or night (1) without needing to call during practice opening hours, which is particularly convenient for clients who work during the day (1)
Clients can see all available appointment slots at a glance (1) and choose a time that suits them rather than being offered limited options by a receptionist (1)

Automated reminder notifications via email or SMS can be sent to clients before their appointment (1) reducing the likelihood of missed appointments and the associated frustration for both the client and the practice (1)
Clients can complete registration and pet health information online before the appointment (1) saving time on arrival and ensuring the vet has relevant information to hand (1)

topic: E2.3 and E2.4 Data collection — accuracy and reliability
scenario: Cranbourne Foods is a food manufacturer that is developing a new range of ready meals. Before launching, the marketing team needs to understand consumer preferences and attitudes to price, portion size and packaging.
question: Explain two reasons why Cranbourne Foods should use both primary and secondary data in its consumer research.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for each reason identified and one mark for a linked expansion, up to a maximum of four marks.
points: Primary data collected directly from target consumers (e.g. through focus groups or surveys) will be specific to Cranbourne's new products (1) providing accurate, relevant insights into preferences for this exact range rather than general market trends (1)

Secondary data from published market research or industry reports can provide broad context about the ready meal market at lower cost (1) saving time and resource compared with collecting all data from scratch through primary methods (1)

Secondary data alone may be too general or outdated to inform decisions about a specific new product (1) so primary data is needed to address the specific questions about Cranbourne's particular target consumers and product concepts (1)
Combining both types allows findings to be cross-referenced (1) increasing confidence that the research conclusions are reliable and not based on a single, potentially biased source (1)
